## 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's Log, Malmstrom, 7 to 19 November 1975

24th NORAD Region Senior Director's Log, Malmstrom, 7 to 19 November 1975 is a document on the board; board tier B, documented channel and capability, programme role indicated but not yet nailed to a primary source; dates 1975-11-07 to 1975-11-19; axes C1 A3 D1; 5 connections.

In one line: Continuous air defence controllers' log of missile-field reports, radar tracks, F-106 scrambles and negatives; released over the signature of a USAF colonel.

### What it is

A WORKING OPERATIONAL LOG, WHICH IS WHY IT IS WORTH MORE THAN ANY REPORT. The 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's Log at Malmstrom AFB records thirteen days of reports from the 341st Strategic Missile Wing's field in the controllers' own shorthand, timed in Zulu, with site designators, radar track numbers, height-finder readings and aircraft call-outs. It was released under FOIA over the signature block 'TERRENCE C. JAMES, Colonel, USAF, Director of Administration', with copies to HQ USAF/DAD and HQ USAF/JACL, and the extracted pages carry stamps 450, 451 and 452 plus a control number 000974, showing that it is a fragment of a much larger paginated release. The log is not an advocate's document and does not read like one: alongside the sightings it records that surveillance could detect no track except known traffic, that an airline crew reported a meteor, and that on 12 November the controllers never had any contact on radar at all. It also contains the 10 November entry naming Minot Air Force Station rather than Minot AFB, which is the one unresolved naming problem in the 1975 sequence. NOTE THE ARCHIVE ITEM IS MISTITLED: it is filed as 'Malmstrom Air Force Base Incident - March 16, 1967 NORAD logs' and its contents are the November 1975 log.

### Why it holds its tier

Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 466 of 1159, score 32). 5 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C1/A3/D1.

### The claims on the record

- **Tier 1 documented.** Its 10 November entry names a different installation from the one CINCNORAD's summary message names nine days later: 'UFO sighting reported by Minot Air Force Station... Approximately 1120Z the object passed over the radar station.' CINCNORAD's message of 11 November 1975 lists 'Minot AFB, ND'. Source: 24th NORAD Region Senior Directors Log, 10 November 1975, against the CINCNORAD message as excerpted at http://www.nicap.org/intsac.htm, both opened 2026-09-19
- **Tier 1 documented.** THE ARCHIVE ITEM IS MISTITLED AND THE BOARD SHOULD SAY SO. The archive.org item is captioned 'Malmstrom Air Force Base Incident - March 16, 1967 NORAD logs'. Its contents are the 24th NORAD Region Senior Director's Log for 7 to 19 November 1975 and it contains nothing about 16 March 1967. Anyone citing this item for the 1967 Echo Flight incident is citing the wrong document. Source: Full text read by this session, https://archive.org/download/MalmstromAirForceBaseIncident/Malmstrom%20Air%20Force%20Base%20Incident%20%E2%80%93%20March%2016,%201967%20NORAD%20logs_djvu.txt, opened 2026-09-19
- **Tier 1 documented.** The log records its own negatives as readily as its sightings: after the 7 Nov 1327Z entry, 'all this time, surveillance has not been able to detect any sort of track except for known traffic'; on 9 Nov at 0320Z the FAA watch supervisor reporting United Flight 157 seeing a meteor; and on 12 Nov at 0251Z 'Never had any joy (contact) on radar.' Its final entry is marked in the original as the last pertaining to these incidents. Source: 24th NORAD Region Senior Directors Log, https://archive.org/download/MalmstromAirForceBaseIncident/Malmstrom%20Air%20Force%20Base%20Incident%20%E2%80%93%20March%2016,%201967%20NORAD%20logs_djvu.txt, opened 2026-09-19
- **Tier 1 documented.** The release attestation reads 'TERRENCE C. JAMES, Colonel, USAF, Director of Administration', with 'Cy to: HQ USAF/DAD, HQ USAF/JACL'. The extracted pages carry stamps 450, 451 and 452 and a control number 000974, establishing that the log is an extract from a larger paginated FOIA compilation of at least 452 pages. Source: 24th NORAD Region Senior Directors Log as released, https://archive.org/download/MalmstromAirForceBaseIncident/Malmstrom%20Air%20Force%20Base%20Incident%20%E2%80%93%20March%2016,%201967%20NORAD%20logs_djvu.txt, opened 2026-09-19

## DoD special access programme governance change, 5 January 1994

DoD special access programme governance change, 5 January 1994 is a event on the board; board tier B, documented channel and capability, programme role indicated but not yet nailed to a primary source; dates 1994-01-05; axes C2 A3 D1; 5 connections.

In one line: SAPOC, Senior Review Group and SAPCO stood up under the Deputy Secretary of Defense.

### What it is

On 5 January 1994 the Deputy Secretary of Defense changed the Department's special access programme management and control structures, standardising the approval, termination, revalidation and restructuring of SAPs through a Special Access Program Oversight Committee chaired by the Deputy Secretary, with a Senior Review Group established to support the SAPOC principals and a Special Access Program Coordinating Office staffing both. By November 1994 the committee was chaired by Deputy Secretary John Deutch with the Under Secretary for Acquisition and Technology, the Under Secretary for Policy, the Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the Assistant Secretary for C3I as permanent, non-delegable members. The Joint Security Commission, reporting to the Secretary of Defense and the Director of Central Intelligence on 28 February 1994, described the committee as recently formed and supported it. This node exists because the board's sapoc node dates the committee to a 2010 directive, and the 2010 issuance re-established rather than created it.

### Why it holds its tier

Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 248 of 1159, score 42). 5 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C2/A3/D1.

### The claims on the record

- **Tier 1 documented.** A central Army special-access oversight office predates the 1994 reform by ten years. GAO/NSIAD-88-152 records: 'A DOD review of Army special access programs in 1983 revealed systemic weaknesses in various management areas, which resulted in establishment of a central oversight office in September 1984.' The same report states that in 1988 'The Deputy Under Secretary of Defense for Policy is required to maintain a listing of all special access programs, but does not do so because of security concerns', and that 'the Secretary's Office has no centralized office with cognizance of all special access programs'. The January 1994 dates this board carries stand; the Army aftermath began in 1983-84. Source: GAO/NSIAD-88-152, B-230522, 24 May 1988, Results in Brief and Recommendations, https://www.gao.gov/assets/nsiad-88-152.pdf
- **Tier 1 documented.** A commission chartered by the Secretary of Defense and the Director of Central Intelligence corroborated the formation within two months: 'Until recently there has been no procedure for centralized assessment of special program proposals submitted directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense by the military departments. The recent formation of the DoD Special Access Program Oversight Committee, which the Commission fully supports, will ensure that every program is reviewed by a panel of senior officials prior to its establishment, and annually thereafter, to determine whether compartmentation for each program is still required.' Source: Joint Security Commission, 'Redefining Security: A Report to the Secretary of Defense and the Director of Central Intelligence', 28 February 1994, chapter 2, https://sgp.fas.org/library/jsc/chap2.html
- **Tier 1 documented.** The same chapter records the scale and the carve-outs the board's oversight view argues from: 'Some of the most sensitive DoD programs are "waived" or "carved out" from certain oversight and administrative requirements. There are over one hundred DoD SAPs, with many having numerous compartments and subcompartments', and each SAP manager 'is free to establish the security rules that will apply to his or her particular program.' On congressional reporting the Commission concluded it saw 'no need to modify existing reporting procedures'. Source: Joint Security Commission, 'Redefining Security', 28 February 1994, chapter 2, https://sgp.fas.org/library/jsc/chap2.html
- **Tier 2 named person on the record.** The annual review and the decision authority date from this change, not from the 2010 directive: 'All SAPs will be reviewed and validated annually for continued SAP status by the OSD SAPOC. ... The DEPSECDEF is the final decision maker in establishing, disestablishing or restructuring SAPs.' Source: Deputy Secretary of Defense, SAPOC Information Bulletin, November 1994, https://sgp.fas.org/othergov/sapoc.html
- **Tier 2 named person on the record.** The change and its date: 'On January 5th, 1994, the Deputy Secretary of Defense (DEPSECDEF) significantly enhanced changes in the DoD Special Access Program (SAP) management and control structures. ... The plan standardized and formalized the SAP approval, termination, revalidation and restructuring process through the Special Access Program Oversight Committee (SAPOC). A Senior Review Group (SRG) was established to support the SAPOC principals.' - **Tier 2 named person on the record.** The committee's membership in November 1994: 'The SAPOC is chaired by the Honorable John Deutch, DEPSECDEF, with permanent members the Honorable Paul Kaminski USD(A&T), the Honorable Walter Slocombe USD(P), ADM William A. Owens, VCJCS, and the Honorable Emmett Paige Jr., ASD(C3I). BGEN Mike Kostelnik, OUSD(A&T), serves as both member and executive secretary to the SAPOC in his capacity as director of the SAPCO (SAP Coordinating Office). SAPOC membership is not further delegable.' Source: Deputy Secretary of Defense, SAPOC Information Bulletin, November 1994, https://sgp.fas.org/othergov/sapoc.html

## DoDD 5205.07, Special Access Program (SAP) Policy (1 Jul 2010, Chg 2 of 4 Feb 2020)

DoDD 5205.07, Special Access Program (SAP) Policy (1 Jul 2010, Chg 2 of 4 Feb 2020) is a document on the board; board tier A, named in sworn testimony or primary documents as directly inside the programme; dates 2010-07-01 to 2024-09-12; axes C1 A3 D2; 5 connections.

In one line: dod-issuance.

### What it is

This is the version of DoD's SAP charter that governed for the entire period covered by the Elizondo, Grusch and Kirkpatrick record, and it is the version cross-referenced by the NISPOM rule at 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3). It reissued the 5 January 2006 directive, established the Special Access Program Oversight Committee, established the DoD SAP Central Office under the authority, direction and control of the Deputy Secretary of Defense, and set out in plain language the three things this board most needs documented. First, the taxonomy: its glossary defines an acknowledged SAP as one 'whose existence is acknowledged but its specific details (technologies, materials, techniques, etc.) are classified'; an unacknowledged SAP as one 'having protective controls ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized for such information'; and a waived SAP as 'A SAP for which the Secretary of Defense has waived applicable reporting in accordance with Reference (c) following a determination of adverse effect to national security. An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls.' Reference (c) is section 119 of title 10. Second, the congressional access rule: members of the defense and intelligence committees are authorised access to DoD SAPs 'except for waived programs', and for waived SAPs 'only the chair, the ranking minority member, and the staff directors' are authorised access unless the Secretary or Deputy Secretary approves otherwise. Third, the custody rule: 'All waived SAP material submitted to Congress, to include annual reports and other products, shall remain in DoD custody. No copies shall be stored outside DoD repositories or control without the approval of the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense.' A committee briefed on a waived program is not permitted to keep the paper.

### Why it holds its tier

Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 63 of 1159, score 74). 6 connections, 2 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C1/A3/D2.

## DoDD 5205.07, DoD Special Access Program (SAP) Policy (12 Sep 2024)

DoDD 5205.07, DoD Special Access Program (SAP) Policy (12 Sep 2024) is a document on the board; board tier A, named in sworn testimony or primary documents as directly inside the programme; dates 2024-09-12; axes C1 A3 D2; 5 connections.

In one line: dod-issuance.

### What it is

The current directive, effective 12 September 2024, cancels the 1 July 2010 version as amended and incorporates the Deputy Secretary of Defense memorandum 'Implementation Guidance for DoD Special Access Program Enterprise Reform' of 11 July 2023. Two changes matter for this board. First, the governance structure is retained and strengthened: the SAPOC remains 'the senior governing body of the DoD SAP Enterprise for governance, management, and oversight of DoD SAPs', chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense, with the Director of DoD SAPCO as Executive Secretary of the SAPOC and the SRG and Chair of the SSWG, reporting directly to the Deputy Secretary. Establishment of new SAP umbrellas and compartments is stated to be 'by exception' and requires Secretary or Deputy Secretary approval. Second, and much more significant, the 2024 directive replaces the acknowledged / unacknowledged / waived taxonomy with two new categories - 'Joint Force Integration SAP', defined as 'A SAP intended for greater integration and sharing across the Joint Force and the broader SAP community', and 'Strategic Enabler SAP', defined as 'A SAP protecting capabilities or information that enable strategic competition and warrant more limited and restrictive sharing'. The words acknowledged, unacknowledged, waived and carve-out do not appear in its definitions section. This does not repeal 10 U.S.C. 119(e), which continues to authorise the reporting waiver, and it does not repeal 32 CFR 117.6(b)(3), which continues to authorise the carve-out and still cites this very directive by number. The effect is that the two mechanisms most relevant to a concealed program survive in statute and in the Code of Federal Regulations while ceasing to be defined in the Department's own public charter - the terminology has been removed from the shop window without being removed from the shop. The directive also carries forward the congressional-contact reporting rule: 'All personnel accessed to DoD SAPs will notify the Director, DoD SAPCO ... when briefing or providing DoD SAP material to any member of Congress.'

### Why it holds its tier

Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 86 of 1159, score 68). 6 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 2 official denials recorded against it. Axes C1/A3/D2.

### The claims on the record

- **Tier 1 documented.** CONTRACTOR SPEECH RESTRICTION. The directive states that no DoD contractor entity 'will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval.' The Director, DoD SAPCO is designated the primary point of contact for congressional SAP matters and 'Maintains records of DoD SAP information provided to Congress.' Source: https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodd/520507p.pdf
- **Tier 1 documented.** DoDD 5205.07 (12 September 2024) cancels DoD Directive 5205.07 of 1 July 2010, as amended, and incorporates the Deputy Secretary of Defense Memorandum, 'Implementation Guidance for DoD Special Access Program Enterprise Reform', 11 July 2023. Source: DoDD 5205.07, 12 September 2024, cover page
- **Tier 1 documented.** DoDD 5205.07 (2024) defines 'Joint Force Integration SAP' as 'A SAP intended for greater integration and sharing across the Joint Force and the broader SAP community' and 'Strategic Enabler SAP' as 'A SAP protecting capabilities or information that enable strategic competition and warrant more limited and restrictive sharing.' Source: DoDD 5205.07, 12 September 2024, Glossary G.2
- **Tier 1 documented.** DoDD 5205.07 (2024) describes the SAPOC as 'the senior governing body of the DoD SAP Enterprise for governance, management, and oversight of DoD SAPs', chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense. Source: DoDD 5205.07, 12 September 2024, section 3.2.a
- **Tier 1 documented.** DoDD 5205.07 (2024) makes the Director, DoD SAPCO the 'primary point of contact for SAP matters with ... the Legislative Branch' and requires that 'All personnel accessed to DoD SAPs will notify the Director, DoD SAPCO ... when briefing or providing DoD SAP material to any member of Congress.' Source: DoDD 5205.07, 12 September 2024, Director DoD SAPCO responsibilities
- **Tier 1 documented.** DoDD 5205.07 (2024) section 3.1.d: 'Establishment of new SAP umbrellas and compartments will be by exception. Establishment ... requires Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense approval.' Source: DoDD 5205.07, 12 September 2024, section 3.1.d
- **Tier 1 documented.** Header block: DoD Directive 5205.07, 'Special Access Program Policy'; effective September 12, 2024; releasability 'Cleared for public release'; 'Reissues and Cancels: DoD Directive 5205.07, July 1, 2010, as amended'; approved by Kathleen H. Hicks, Deputy Secretary of Defense. Source: https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodd/520507p.pdf

## DoD OIG - Evaluation of the DoD's Actions Regarding Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (DODIG-2023-109)

DoD OIG - Evaluation of the DoD's Actions Regarding Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (DODIG-2023-109) is a document on the board; board tier A, named in sworn testimony or primary documents as directly inside the programme; dates 2023 to 2024; axes C1 A3 D3; 5 connections.

In one line: Classified report 15 Aug 2023; unclassified summary released 25 Jan 2024.

### What it is

The Inspector General's evaluation of how the Department handles UAP, completed 15 August 2023 and released in unclassified summary on 25 January 2024. The full report is classified; the public has the summary only. Its findings are structural and damning in an undramatic way: the Department has no overarching UAP policy; different DoD components each developed their own separate processes for collecting, analysing and identifying UAP incidents; and as a result the Department cannot ensure that national security and flight safety threats from UAP have been identified and addressed. It made eleven recommendations to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security, the service secretaries and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, including development of a department-wide policy to integrate UAP roles, responsibilities, requirements and coordination procedures into existing intelligence, counterintelligence and force protection policies. For this board the finding that matters is the fragmentation one. An office that formally reviews only what it can reach, inside a department the IG says has no unified UAP process and component-level stovepipes, cannot produce a negative finding of departmental scope - and every AARO negative finding since has been phrased as 'AARO has discovered no evidence', which is a statement about AARO's reach, not the Department's contents. The classification of the full report means the IG's own account of where the stovepipes are remains unavailable, including through PURSUE.

### Why it holds its tier

Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 79 of 1159, score 69). 6 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 1 official denial recorded against it. Axes C1/A3/D3.

### The claims on the record

- **Tier 1 documented.** Consequence finding: 'We determined that the DoD has no overarching UAP policy and, as a result, it lacks assurance that national security and flight safety threats to the United States from UAP have been identified and mitigated.' Source: https://media.defense.gov/2024/Jan/25/2003381266/-1/-1/1/UNCLASSIFIED%20SUMMARY_UNIDENTIFIED%20ANOMALOUS%20PHENOMENA%20SECURE.PDF
- **Tier 1 documented.** DODIG-2023-109, dated 15 August 2023, evaluated how the DoD, military services, defense agencies and counterintelligence organizations detect, report, collect, analyze and identify UAP; the unclassified summary was released 25 January 2024. Source: DoD OIG report page and press release
- **Tier 1 documented.** On the absence of a response plan: 'The DoD has not issued a comprehensive UAP response plan that identifies roles, responsibilities, requirements, and coordination procedures... As a result, the DoD response to UAP incidents is uncoordinated and concentrated within each Military Department. Officials from the Military Services and MDCOs stated that they have been waiting for the DoD to issue comprehensive UAP guidance before developing their own guidance.' Source: https://media.defense.gov/2024/Jan/25/2003381266/-1/-1/1/UNCLASSIFIED%20SUMMARY_UNIDENTIFIED%20ANOMALOUS%20PHENOMENA%20SECURE.PDF
- **Tier 1 documented.** Recommendation 1: 'We recommend that the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security, in coordination with the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office Director, issue a Department of Defense policy to integrate unidentified anomalous phenomena roles, responsibilities, requirements, and coordination procedures into existing intelligence, counterintelligence, and force protection policies and procedures. The policy should include methods to address unidentified anomalous phenomena incidents and should align with policies and procedures for the protection of United States persons' civil liberties.' USD(I&S) and the AARO Director agreed; the recommendation was left 'resolved but open'. Source: https://media.defense.gov/2024/Jan/25/2003381266/-1/-1/1/UNCLASSIFIED%20SUMMARY_UNIDENTIFIED%20ANOMALOUS%20PHENOMENA%20SECURE.PDF
- **Tier 1 documented.** The DoD IG found the Department lacks a comprehensive, coordinated approach to UAP and had not issued a comprehensive UAP response plan. Source: DODIG-2023-109 unclassified summary, January 2024
- **Tier 1 documented.** The IG found DoD does not formally require components to report UAP incidents to AARO, and that reporting systems differ across services including the Air Force's Marauder system. Source: DODIG-2023-109 unclassified summary
- **Tier 1 documented.** The IG found geographic combatant commanders were largely excluded from UAP policy development despite bearing statutory responsibility for threat detection. Source: DODIG-2023-109 unclassified summary
- **Tier 1 documented.** The IG found that DoD lacks an overarching UAP policy, that components developed separate processes, and that the Department cannot ensure national security and flight safety threats from UAP have been identified and addressed. Source: DoD OIG press release on DODIG-2023-109

## DoDM 5205.07, DoD SAP Security Manual (Volumes 1-4)

DoDM 5205.07, DoD SAP Security Manual (Volumes 1-4) is a document on the board; board tier A, named in sworn testimony or primary documents as directly inside the programme; dates 2012-01-01; axes C1 A3 D1; 5 connections.

In one line: dod-issuance.

### What it is

The DoD SAP Security Manual is issued in four volumes under number 5205.07: Volume 1, General Procedures (18 June 2015, Change 1 12 February 2018); Volume 2, Personnel Security; Volume 3, Physical Security; and Volume 4, Marking. Volume 1 is the volume that carries the carve-out definition and the DSS relief provision, and is the only volume this board has been able to obtain in full from an archived copy of the DoD Issuances site; the current live URLs at esd.whs.mil for volumes 1 through 4 return errors to unauthenticated retrieval as of 12 August 2026, which is itself a finding worth recording. Volume 1 states its own lineage: it 'Assigns responsibilities, implements policy established in DoD Instruction (DoDI) 5205.11 ... and describes the general procedures for the administration of DoD SAP security' and 'Incorporates and cancels Revision 1 Department of Defense Overprint to the National Industrial Security Program (NISP) Operating Manual Supplement'. That last clause is the historical bridge: the security rules for contractor SAPs used to live as an overprint to the NISPOM Supplement, i.e. as a special-case annex to the industrial security system, and were pulled out into a standalone DoD manual - moving contractor SAP security further from the NISP baseline that DCSA inspects.

### Why it holds its tier

Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 66 of 1159, score 73). 5 connections, 4 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C1/A3/D1.

### The claims on the record

- **Tier 1 documented.** DoDM 5205.07 Vol 1 glossary: 'carve-out. A provision approved by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense that relieves DSS of its NISP obligation to perform industrial security oversight functions for a DoD SAP.' Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20191018064106/https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodm/520507_vol1.pdf
- **Tier 1 documented.** DoDM 5205.07 Vol 2, para 5 (Polygraphs): 'The Deputy Secretary of Defense is the approval authority for the use of polygraph examination as a mandatory access determination requirement; the requirement must be consistently applied to all candidates in accordance with DoDI 5210.91. CI-Scope polygraph examination must not be used as the only basis for granting access to DoD SAPs. Exceptions to these requirements will only be granted by the Deputy Secretary of Defense. ... CI polygraph examinations are considered current when administered within the past 5 years.' Para 6 provides that 'CA SAPCOs may establish or authorize SAP billet structures or access quotas that assign individual access by organization and duty position to SAPs under their cognizance.' Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20250305140253/https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodm/520507_vol2.pdf
- **Tier 1 documented.** DoDM 5205.07 Volume 1 applies to all DoD Components, to 'All DoD Component contractors and consultants who require access to DoD SAPs pursuant to the terms and conditions of the contract or agreement', and to non-DoD USG entities requiring access under an MOA. Source: DoDM 5205.07 Volume 1, para 2
- **Tier 1 documented.** DoDM 5205.07 Volume 1 states that it 'Incorporates and cancels Revision 1 Department of Defense Overprint to the National Industrial Security Program (NISP) Operating Manual Supplement.' Source: DoDM 5205.07 Volume 1, para 1.a(2)
- **Tier 1 documented.** THE CARVE-OUT'S OPERATIONAL CONTENT. DoDM 5205.07 Vol 1, Enclosure 2, para 2 (Director, DSS): 'Unless a carve-out provision is approved by the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense: (1) Performs SAP security inspections at cleared defense contractor locations in accordance with this volume, Reference (f), and the government contracting activity's completed DD Form 254 ... (2) Authorizes classified contractor SAP information systems (ISs) and the introduction of guest systems in contractor SAP facilities (SAPFs). (3) Coordinates with the designated counterintelligence (CI) component to provide cross-sharing of threat and incident information affecting the security of the facility or its defense information or cleared personnel.' A carve-out removes all three functions at once: physical inspection, IT accreditation, and CI information sharing. Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20191018064106/https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodm/520507_vol1.pdf
- **Tier 1 documented.** Vol 1 physical-security/visitor rules acknowledge the existence of undisclosed sites in operative text: 'Federal Government-affiliated identification cards will not be used for positive identification in unacknowledged locations.' Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20191018064106/https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodm/520507_vol1.pdf
- **Tier 1 documented.** Vol 1 states that inspections 'will be coordinated among the SAPCOs and DSS when not carved out and conducted jointly to the greatest extent possible' -- confirming that when a SAP IS carved out, the only remaining inspection is the program's own self-inspection plus SAPCO-internal compliance inspection. Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20191018064106/https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodm/520507_vol1.pdf
- **Tier 1 documented.** Vol 1, Enclosure 4, para 4: 'The CUA documents areas of authorities and responsibilities between cognizant security offices (CSOs) when they share the same SAPF. ... The first CSO in an area, unless otherwise agreed upon, will be considered the host CSO responsible for all security oversight.' And, critically: 'For CUAs, the responsible organization will be identified for executing security cognizance with a carved-out SAP.' Multiple SAPs -- including carved-out ones -- can lawfully co-occupy one accredited facility under a written host/tenant agreement. Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20191018064106/https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodm/520507_vol1.pdf

## DoDM 5205.07 Volume 1, DoD SAP Security Manual: General Procedures

DoDM 5205.07 Volume 1, DoD SAP Security Manual: General Procedures is a document on the board; board tier A, named in sworn testimony or primary documents as directly inside the programme; dates 2015-06-18; axes C1 A3 D2; 5 connections.

In one line: dod-issuance.

### What it is

Volume 1 of the four-volume DoD SAP Security Manual assigns responsibilities and describes the general procedures for the administration of DoD SAP security, implementing the policy of DoDI 5205.11, and it incorporates and cancels the Revision 1 Department of Defense Overprint to the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual Supplement. Its Enclosure 2 contains the operative statement of what a carve-out removes. The Director, DSS - the office now called the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency - administers the NISP and issues facility clearances for defense contractors 'to include contractors performing on DoD SAPs'; but then, 'Unless a carve-out provision is approved by the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense', the Director performs SAP security inspections at cleared defense contractor locations, authorises classified contractor SAP information systems and the introduction of guest systems in contractor SAP facilities, and coordinates with the designated counterintelligence component to cross-share threat and incident information. Read the sentence backwards and it is an inventory of what disappears when a carve-out is signed: the independent physical inspection, the independent accreditation of the computers, and the independent counterintelligence feed. Its glossary supplies the definition in eleven words of substance: 'carve-out. A provision approved by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense that relieves DSS of its NISP obligation to perform industrial security oversight functions for a DoD SAP.' Volume 1 also documents two cover mechanisms - HANDLE VIA SPECIAL ACCESS CHANNELS ONLY (HVSACO), an unclassified handling caveat used among other things 'When using a SAP nickname for an unacknowledged SAP', and the rule that 'Federal Government-affiliated identification cards will not be used for positive identification in unacknowledged locations'.

### Why it holds its tier

Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 110 of 1159, score 60). 5 connections, 2 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 1 official denial recorded against it. Axes C1/A3/D2.

### The claims on the record

- **Tier 1 documented.** DoDM 5205.07-V1 Enclosure 10 provides that 'Federal Government-affiliated identification cards will not be used for positive identification in unacknowledged locations.' Source: DoDM 5205.07 Volume 1, Enclosure 10, para 5
- **Tier 1 documented.** DoDM 5205.07-V1 Enclosure 2 para 2.c: 'Unless a carve-out provision is approved by the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense: (1) Performs SAP security inspections at cleared defense contractor locations ... (2) Authorizes classified contractor SAP information systems (ISs) and the introduction of guest systems in contractor SAP facilities (SAPFs). ## Estimate of the Situation (1948)

Estimate of the Situation (1948) is a document on the board; board tier B, documented channel and capability, programme role indicated but not yet nailed to a primary source; dates 1948; axes C1 A3 D2; 5 connections.

In one line: Top Secret Project SIGN assessment; destroyed.

### What it is

In mid-1948 the Project SIGN staff at Wright Field completed a Top Secret document, in the standard military 'estimate of the situation' format, concluding that the objects under investigation were interplanetary in origin. It went up the chain to Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Hoyt Vandenberg, who rejected it on the grounds that it lacked proof and directed that copies be destroyed. No copy has ever surfaced. This board treats the Estimate as the single most consequential missing document of the twentieth century on this subject, and its status is stronger than folklore: the Condon Report, commissioned and paid for by the Air Force under contract 44620-67-C-0035, states in Section V Chapter 2 that the estimate was prepared, that Vandenberg rejected it, and that copies were destroyed. Edward Ruppelt, the first Blue Book director, published the same account in 1956 from personal knowledge. Against this, Air Force spokesmen and members of Congress have at times asserted no such estimate ever existed. The conflict is itself the datum: the government's own contracted history records a document the government elsewhere denies. It also establishes, twenty years before the Bolender memo and forty-seven before the GAO records finding, that destruction was the standard disposition for adverse conclusions.

### Why it holds its tier

Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 336 of 1159, score 37). 5 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 1 official denial recorded against it. Axes C1/A3/D2.

### The claims on the record

- **Tier 1 documented.** 'Staff members prepared a classified Estimate of the Situation in July 1948 asserting UFOs were interplanetary vehicles. Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Vandenberg rejected it for lacking proof, and copies were destroyed.' Source: Condon Report, Section V Chapter 2, 'UFOs 1947-1968' (University of Colorado, USAF contract 44620-67-C-0035, 1968)
- **Tier 2 named person on the record.** Air Force representatives and Rep. L. Mendel Rivers have asserted that no such Estimate ever existed. Source: Congressional and Air Force statements catalogued in the secondary literature on Project SIGN
- **Tier 2 named person on the record.** Ruppelt first published the existence, content and destruction of the Estimate in 1956 based on his tenure as Blue Book director. Source: Ruppelt, 'The Report on Unidentified Flying Objects', 1956
- **Tier 3 stated inference.** A government-contracted official report and official denials cannot both be correct; the contracted report was written with access to Air Force files and the denials were made publicly, which favours the report. Source: Inference from the conflict between Condon Sec. V Ch. 2 and later official denials

## Foreign Technology Division, Wright-Patterson AFB

Foreign Technology Division, Wright-Patterson AFB is a institution on the board; board tier B, documented channel and capability, programme role indicated but not yet nailed to a primary source; dates 1961-07-01 to 1991; axes C2 A3 D1; 5 connections.

In one line: Air Force Systems Command foreign materiel exploitation centre, 1961-1991; the office that held Project Blue Book.

### What it is

The Foreign Technology Division was the Air Force's foreign aerospace materiel exploitation centre at Wright-Patterson AFB, sitting between the Air Technical Intelligence Center and the National Air and Space Intelligence Center in the same lineage and at the same station. Air Force Regulation 80-17 of 19 September 1966 assigned it the Blue Book effort in its own name: FTD analysed and evaluated every report a base could not identify, and wrote the final case report on each. The USAF Scientific Advisory Board's ad hoc review committee of March 1966 called it the cognizant Air Force agency for UFO sightings and recommended it keep the job, while recording that the whole programme ran on one officer, a sergeant and a secretary. The board carries this organisation in prose twenty-one times and has never had a node for it.

Source: Air Force Regulation 80-17, 19 September 1966, https://nicap.org/afr80-17.htm
- **Tier 1 documented.** The Blue Book effort was assigned to FTD by regulation: 'The Air Force Systems Command will support the program with current resources within the Foreign Technology Division (FTD) at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, to continue Blue Book effort.' - **Tier 1 documented.** The USAF Scientific Advisory Board's ad hoc committee of March 1966 identified FTD as 'the AFSC Foreign Technology Division, which is the cognizant Air Force agency that collates information on UFO sightings and monitors investigations of individual cases', and recommended that it 'should continue to exercise its presently assigned responsibilities concerning UFOs.' ## Death of Frank R. Olson, 1953, and the compensation and litigation that followed

Death of Frank R. Olson, 1953, and the compensation and litigation that followed is a event on the board; board tier B, documented channel and capability, programme role indicated but not yet nailed to a primary source; dates 1953-11-19 to 2013-07-17; axes C0 A1 D3; 5 connections.

In one line: Army civilian dosed with LSD without his knowledge at a CIA meeting on 19 November 1953; died in New York days later; compensated by Private Law 94-126 in 1976; the family's 2012 suit dismissed in D.D.C. in 2013.

### What it is

This is the one death inside a compartmented American programme that the government conceded, compensated by statute, and then litigated over sixty years later, and it belongs on this board because the paper trail exists on both sides. Frank R. Olson, a civilian employee of the Army at Fort Detrick, was given LSD without his knowledge in a bottle of Cointreau at a CIA and Army meeting on 19 November 1953 and died in New York within about a week. The Rockefeller Commission disclosed the connection in June 1975 without naming him, and attached to its own account a footnote saying the few remaining Agency records indicate he may have had a history of emotional instability. Congress paid his widow and three children $187,500 each in 1976 in exchange for a full waiver, and President Ford signed it saying his administration had wanted twice that. In 2012 two of the children sued the United States alleging the death was a murder concealed for sixty years; the District of Columbia dismissed the suit in 2013 on timeliness, the 1976 waiver and sovereign immunity, while recording that the public record supports many of the allegations. Four opened records disagree about which floor he fell from, what day he died and whether anyone was reprimanded.

### Why it holds its tier

Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 219 of 1159, score 44). 5 connections, 2 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 1 official denial recorded against it. Axes C0/A1/D3.

Olson, Lisa Olson Hayward, Eric Olson, and Nils Olson, in full settlement of all of their claims against the United States arising out of the death of Doctor Frank R. Olson in November 1953, if all of them waive any and all rights arising out of such death.' Source: Private Law 94-126, 90 Stat. 3006 (1976), quoted in full in Olson v. United States, No. 12-1924 (JEB), D.D.C., memorandum opinion of 17 July 2013, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCOURTS-dcd-1_12-cv-01924/pdf/USCOURTS-dcd-1_12-cv-01924-0.pdf
- **Tier 1 documented.** President Ford signed the bill on 12 October 1976 and stated the administration's own position on the amount: 'Legislation to appropriate $1,250,000 to compensate the wife and three children of Dr. Olson for his death was supported by this administration. However, the Congress approved a measure calling for the payment of a total of $750,000 to these survivors.' Source: Gerald R. Ford, Statement on Signing the Bill Providing for the Relief of the Survivors of Dr. Frank R. Olson, 12 October 1976, https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/statement-signing-the-bill-providing-for-the-relief-the-survivors-dr-frank-r-olson

## Fleet Forces Command 'URGENT SAFETY OF FLIGHT ISSUE' Email (Jan 2015, recalled)

Fleet Forces Command 'URGENT SAFETY OF FLIGHT ISSUE' Email (Jan 2015, recalled) is a document on the board; board tier B, documented channel and capability, programme role indicated but not yet nailed to a primary source; dates 2015; axes C1 A3 D3; 5 connections.

In one line: Recalled Navy fleet-wide safety message carrying the GO FAST video.

### What it is

A January 2015 email from the operations officer of US Fleet Forces Command to all subordinate commanders, subject line 'URGENT SAFETY OF FLIGHT ISSUE,' attaching the GO FAST video and asking: 'If any of you know what these are, tell me ASAP. We are having multiple near-midair collisions, and if we do not resolve it soon, we will have to shut down the exercise.' Then-Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet, at the time Commander of Naval Meteorology and Oceanography Command, testified in writing to the House Oversight joint subcommittees on 13 November 2024 that the email disappeared from his account and from other recipients' accounts 'without explanation' the very next day, and that he concluded the information 'must have been classified within a special access program managed by an intelligence agency.' This document - or rather its deletion - is the single sharpest artefact of the concealment mechanism in the aviator record. It is not a classification decision anyone defended, not a refusal to comment, not a denial: it is the retroactive removal of an official Navy flight-safety warning from every recipient's inbox. No agency has acknowledged ordering it, and the message identifier, sender and recall authority remain unidentified.

### The board's reading

The recalled January 2015 US Fleet Forces Command message is the highest-value single artefact on the aviator strand, and it deserves separate treatment because of what it rules out. A refusal to comment is consistent with indifference. A classification decision is consistent with ordinary secrecy. But the retroactive deletion of an already-distributed fleet-wide flight-safety warning from the inboxes of every subordinate commander is not consistent with either. It requires that someone with authority over Navy messaging systems decided, within 24 hours, that a safety-of-flight warning about repeated near-midair collisions was more dangerous distributed than the near-midairs themselves. Gallaudet, a serving flag officer at the time and later acting NOAA Administrator, drew the only available inference in sworn testimony: the information 'must have been classified within a special access program managed by an intelligence agency.' The message is also the connective tissue between the two halves of the aviator record. It carried GO FAST - one of the three videos DoD later released as authentic and unidentified - and it described exactly the problem Ryan Graves's squadron was filing unacknowledged safety reports about in the same airspace in the same period. Nine years later, AARO reanalysed GO FAST on parallax grounds and concluded it showed nothing anomalous. That analysis, whatever its merits, has no bearing on why the warning was withdrawn. No agency has ever acknowledged withdrawing it, and the sender, message identifier and recall authority remain unidentified.

## Government Accountability Office

Government Accountability Office is a institution on the board; board tier C, contextual, real and relevant, no direct programme linkage on the record yet; dates 1921-07-01; axes C0 A1 D3; 5 connections.

In one line: Legislative branch audit agency; author of the 1995 Roswell records search.

### What it is

GAO is the audit arm of Congress and the only investigative body on this board that answers to the legislature rather than the executive. Its single most important product in this domain is GAO/NSIAD-95-187, 'Government Records: Results of a Search for Records Concerning the 1947 Crash Near Roswell, New Mexico', issued 28 July 1995 at the request of Representative Steven Schiff of New Mexico after the Air Force declined to give him a straight answer. GAO's finding is one of the load-bearing facts of the entire field: that the outgoing messages of Roswell Army Air Field for the period March 1945 to December 1949 had been destroyed, without any destruction certificate being located to authorise it. GAO could not determine who destroyed them or when. That is not a finding that the material existed; it is a finding that the record of the period was not kept in the manner required, at exactly the installation and exactly the period at issue. GAO's involvement also demonstrates the tool Congress has never fully used since: a legislative-branch auditor with statutory access authority, directed at the classification and records-management conduct of the agencies, rather than at the phenomenon.

## GAO accession 130581 - Controls Over Classified Documents for a Special Access Program at Lockheed Corporation

GAO accession 130581 - Controls Over Classified Documents for a Special Access Program at Lockheed Corporation is a document on the board; board tier B, documented channel and capability, programme role indicated but not yet nailed to a primary source; dates 1986-07-24; axes C1 A1 D3; 5 connections.

In one line: GAO testimony, 24 July 1986, House Energy and Commerce, Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations.

### What it is

On 24 July 1986 the General Accounting Office told a congressional subcommittee that a prime contractor's special-access document control had failed, and in the same statement explained that the body which would ordinarily have inspected it had been excluded from doing so since 1965. That conjunction is this board's structural argument, documented and dated. The cover page reads: 'STATEMENT OF MARTIN M FERBER, ASSOCIATE DIRECTOR, NATIONAL SECURITY AND INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS DIVISION, BEFORE THE SUBCOMMITTEE ON OVERSIGHT AND INVESTIGATIONS, HOUSE COMMITTEE ON ENERGY AND COMMERCE, ON CONTROLS OVER CLASSIFIED DOCUMENTS FOR A SPECIAL ACCESS PROGRAM AT LOCKHEED CORPORATION'. The venue is worth noting: not a defence committee.

The numbers are exact and the popular version of them is wrong. Lockheed reported 1,460 discrepancies in an inventory of about 40,000 secret and top-secret items. As of 19 July 1986 it had completed investigation on 235 of them; 224 were 'later accounted for' and 11 were unresolved -- 7 inadvertently destroyed and 4 not located. The 46 destroyed and the 17 transferred out of the company sit inside the 224 that were accounted for, not outside them. The genuinely unaccounted-for total is 11.

GAO explains the carve-out in its own words: special access contracts are 'carved out of the Defense Investigative Service's periodic inspection program', a 1965 decision, and by 1983 GAO estimated 'there probably were several thousand such contracts'. Its closing sentence is the finding: 'it appears inconsistent to us to establish a special access program because of security considerations and then afford it less document protection than normal classified programs.' The companion letter report to the Secretary of Defense, GAO/NSIAD-86-191 of 7 August 1986, goes further and names the plant the testimony would not.

## Los Alamos Green Fireballs Conference

Los Alamos Green Fireballs Conference is a event on the board; board tier B, documented channel and capability, programme role indicated but not yet nailed to a primary source; dates 1949; axes C1 A2 D2; 5 connections.

In one line: 16 February 1949, Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory, New Mexico.

### What it is

The first documented scientific conference convened by the United States government on unexplained aerial objects over its own nuclear installations. Held at Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory on 16 February 1949 and attended by Laboratory Director Norris Bradbury, Edward Teller, Frederick Reines and representatives of the FBI, the Atomic Energy Commission and the US military, it addressed the green fireballs that had been appearing over Los Alamos, Sandia, Kirtland and the surrounding weapons complex since December 1948. Lincoln LaPaz of the University of New Mexico's Institute of Meteoritics had been brought in by Kirtland intelligence officers because the objects superficially resembled meteors; his assessment was that they did not behave like them. Los Alamos National Laboratory confirms the conference took place and that its National Security Research Center holds the minutes. The conclusion recorded was that the fireballs were ultimately dismissed as a national security threat - which did not stop the Air Force establishing Project Twinkle ten months later to instrument them. Newly declassified records were publicised in July 2026. The jurisdictional fact is the durable one: this was handled inside the AEC's contractor-operated laboratory complex, not by the Air Force's public UFO project at Wright-Patterson, and the record ended up in a contractor archive rather than in federal custody.

### Why it holds its tier

Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 426 of 1159, score 33). 5 connections, 2 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C1/A2/D2.

### The claims on the record

- **Tier 1 documented.** A conference was organised at Los Alamos on 16 February 1949 attended by Norris Bradbury, Frederick Reines and Edward Teller with FBI, AEC and US military representatives; the National Security Research Center holds the conference minutes. Source: Los Alamos National Laboratory, 18 November 2024
- **Tier 1 documented.** The conference ultimately dismissed the notion that the green fireballs were a significant national security threat. Source: Los Alamos National Laboratory, 18 November 2024
- **Tier 2 named person on the record.** In December 1949 Project Twinkle, a network of green fireball observation and photographic stations, was established but never fully implemented. Source: Contemporaneous Air Force records; FBI file 62-HQ-83894 material released in the Department of War PURSUE Release 01

## Grusch PPD-19 Urgent Concern Complaint to the ICIG

Grusch PPD-19 Urgent Concern Complaint to the ICIG is a document on the board; board tier B, documented channel and capability, programme role indicated but not yet nailed to a primary source; dates 2022; axes C2 A3 D3; 5 connections.

In one line: Whistleblower complaint, 25 May 2022.

### What it is

The founding document of the modern disclosure record. Filed 25 May 2022 with the Inspector General of the Intelligence Community by Irvin Charles McCullough III - the IC's first Inspector General - on behalf of David Grusch, under Presidential Policy Directive 19 and the urgent-concern statute. It followed an earlier July 2021 protected disclosure by Grusch to the DoD Inspector General. The preponderance of the complaint is classified; Grusch's unclassified characterization under oath is that it concerns 'both material acquisition and exploitation activity' and the withholding of UAP baselining data from the intelligence professionals who brief aircrews. In July 2022 the ICIG determined the complaint credible and urgent, the statutory trigger for transmission to the congressional intelligence committees. A companion reprisal complaint alleges Grusch's identity and his UAP communications with the DoD IG were disclosed outside the IG channel; the unclassified version reported in June 2023 names Avril Haines, Sean Kirkpatrick, Susan Gough, Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand and Rep. Tim Burchett in its account of how the information moved. Grusch testified that the ICIG had no smooth mechanism to route the disclosure to the Armed Services Committees despite Title 10 equities - meaning the substantive Title 10 allegations may never have reached the committees with jurisdiction over the alleged programs.

### The board's reading

Chain of custody for the complaint, as established by sworn testimony and reporting. July 2021: Grusch makes a protected disclosure of classified information to the DoD Inspector General concerning the improper withholding and concealment of UAP-related material from Congress. 25 May 2022: Irvin Charles McCullough III of Compass Rose Legal Group, the first Inspector General of the Intelligence Community, files a PPD-19 urgent-concern complaint with the ICIG on Grusch's behalf. July 2022: the ICIG determines the complaint credible and urgent, the statutory trigger for transmission to the congressional intelligence committees. A companion reprisal complaint alleges Grusch's identity and his DoD IG communications were disclosed to DoD and IC entities outside the IG's office; the unclassified version reported in June 2023 references DNI Avril Haines, AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick, DoD spokesperson Susan Gough, Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand and Rep. Tim Burchett in its account of how the information moved. Grusch's unclassified description of the underlying subject matter, given under oath to Chairman Grothman: 'Both material acquisition and exploitation activity, also baselining the UAPs but not sharing it with, you know, intelligence professionals that are actually doing step briefs to pilots.' He further testified that the preponderance of the complaint was classified, that he knows the exact locations of held material and provided them to the Inspector General and in part to the intelligence committees, and that he had the individuals with firsthand knowledge make their own protected disclosures. He also testified to a routing failure: PPD-19 and ICD 120 send such disclosures to the intelligence committees, and there was no good mechanism for the ICIG to provide his information to the House and Senate Armed Services Committees despite Title 10 equities being at play.

### Why it holds its tier

Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 350 of 1159, score 36). 5 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C2/A3/D3.

- **Tier 1 documented.** Grusch's unclassified description of the complaint's subject: 'Both material acquisition and exploitation activity, also baselining the UAPs but not sharing it with intelligence professionals that are actually doing step briefs to pilots.' Source: House Oversight hearing transcript, 26 July 2023
- **Tier 2 named person on the record.** The reprisal complaint alleges Grusch's identity and his DoD IG communications were disclosed to DoD and IC entities outside the IG's office. Source: Unclassified reprisal complaint reported by Liberation Times, 13 June 2023

## Hospital Regional de Varginha

Hospital Regional de Varginha is a institution on the board; board tier C, contextual, real and relevant, no direct programme linkage on the record yet; dates no dates recorded; axes C0 A0 D0; 5 connections.

In one line: Medical facility.

### What it is

The facility referred to in the Varginha literature as the Hospital Regional de Varginha is registered in Brazil's national health-establishment register, CNES, as the Hospital Regional do Sul de Minas, CNES code 2761041, at Rua Rui Barbosa 158, Centro, Varginha, Minas Gerais (CEP 37002-140), under municipal administration, operating continuous 24-hour service and providing SUS outpatient care. Varginha's other registered hospitals in the same register include the Hospital Bom Pastor, run by the municipal hospital foundation, and the Hospital Unimed Varginha. The hospital is on this board because it is one of the medical facilities named in the January 1996 Varginha case as a place to which an injured creature was reportedly taken and held before being moved on, in the sequence involving military and fire-brigade personnel that is recorded elsewhere on this board as ev-varginha-1996. The case is not a historical curiosity: it was carried to Capitol Hill on its thirtieth anniversary, and on 8 July 2026 a congressional demand went to the CIA and FBI for records on the Varginha and Campinas incidents - meaning that a municipal hospital in Minas Gerais is now a named location in an American records fight. What exists here as verified fact is the facility and its registry entry; the 1996 hospital-custody sequence rests on witness testimony and journalism, not on any hospital record obtained in this pass.

## House Armed Services Committee

House Armed Services Committee is a institution on the board; board tier C, contextual, real and relevant, no direct programme linkage on the record yet; dates 1947; axes C1 A3 D0; 5 connections.

In one line: HASC; conference principal under Chairman Rogers.

### What it is

HASC held the House side of the NDAA conference through the stripping and is the committee whose jurisdiction the Senate's independent Review Board would most directly have displaced. The pattern of what survived tracks committee interest closely: every enacted UAP provision routes its remedy to 'the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership', the defence and intelligence committees, while every removed provision routed authority to an independent agency, to the Archivist acting on a board's direction, or to a court. Sec. 1687, the funding limitation that did survive, is precisely the form of leverage that keeps the armed services committees as the gatekeeper: it does not open anything to the public, it compels description to the committees.

## ICD 906, Controlled Access Programs (ODNI)

ICD 906, Controlled Access Programs (ODNI) is a document on the board; board tier A, named in sworn testimony or primary documents as directly inside the programme; dates 2015-10-17; axes C2 A3 D3; 5 connections.

In one line: ic-directive.

### What it is

ICD 906 is the directive that governs what the intelligence community calls its special access programs. Its authority is 'The National Security Act of 1947, as amended; Executive Order (EO) 12333, as amended; and other applicable provisions of law', and it 'establishes the oversight and management of Intelligence Community (IC) special access programs pursuant to EO 13526, Section 4.3, or any successor document, referred to within the IC as Controlled Access Programs (CAPs)'. The reissued version obtained for this board supersedes the ICD 906 signed 17 October 2015; the released PDF was generated on 19 December 2024 and its signature block is an image that does not resolve to text, so the exact reissue date is not machine-readable in the public copy. The substance is unambiguous and, for this board, extraordinary. Only the DNI or the Principal Deputy DNI may establish, validate, modify or terminate a CAP. CAPs are defined as 'a top-level control system (such as Special Intelligence, Talent Keyhole, Human Intelligence Control System), and any compartment or sub-compartment under a control system'. Unacknowledged CAPs exist and 'may be established only where knowledge of the existence of a program would reveal aspects of its protected information ... Unacknowledged CAPs may be established only with the approval of the DNI or PDDNI'. Governance mirrors DoD: a CAP Oversight Committee chaired by the PDDNI or designee, and a Senior Review Group. All CAPs are to be recorded in Scattered Castles, the IC personnel security database - 'Any exemption from this requirement shall be approved only by the DNI or PDDNI'. Access may be limited by billet or 'by name or position (BYNOP)'. Critically, ICD 906 assigns the ODNI Controlled Access Program Central Office responsibility for 'the coordination of CAP-related engagements, to include, but not limited to, congressional briefings, requests from the Information Security Oversight Office, and the National Security Council' - and nowhere in the directive is there any counterpart to 10 U.S.C. 119: no annual report deadline, no 30-day pre-initiation notice, no statutory list. The IC side of the architecture has less congressional reporting machinery than the DoD side, not more. ICD 906 also expressly does not apply to SAPs established by the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy or Homeland Security or the Attorney General, 'Nor does this Directive apply to special access programs under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action' - identifying, in one sentence, a third category of program governed by neither regime.

### The board's reading

Why the intelligence side is the harder problem and the softer target at the same time. Harder: ICD 906 has no statutory annual report deadline, no 30-day pre-initiation clock and no publicly reported program list, and unacknowledged CAPs may be created on the signature of two people, the DNI or the Principal Deputy DNI. Softer: since 15 March 2022 the statute at 50 U.S.C. 3091a requires semiannual briefings on every controlled access program in effect to the intelligence and appropriations committees and congressional leadership, requires annual reports listing every active and every terminated compartment and sub-compartment with a DNI certification that each is substantiated and justified and a named control officer for each, contains no waiver authority whatsoever, and since 23 December 2024 cuts off National Intelligence Program funding for any CAP established without notification. On paper the IC has the strongest special-access oversight regime in the United States government and the DoD has the weakest. ICD 906 also does two things of direct forensic value: it requires that all CAPs and all individual accesses be recorded in Scattered Castles, the IC personnel security database, with exemptions approvable only by the DNI or PDDNI and reviewed annually - so a person's access history is a queryable record - and it expressly disclaims application to programs 'under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action', identifying the one remaining space that neither SAP regime reaches.

### Why it holds its tier

Re-graded A on a global pass (rank 50 of 1159, score 81). 7 connections, 2 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C2/A3/D3.

## Japan Air Lines flight 1628, Alaska, 17 November 1986

Japan Air Lines flight 1628, Alaska, 17 November 1986 is a event on the board; board tier B, documented channel and capability, programme role indicated but not yet nailed to a primary source; dates 1986-11-17 to 1987-03-05; axes C0 A0 D2; 5 connections.

In one line: A civil-aviation incident with a 1,500-page federal file at the National Archives, an FAA investigation, an agency press release concluding against a second aircraft, and a documented seventeen-year FOIA recovery.

### What it is

THIS IS THE NODE IN THIS CLUSTER WITH A REAL AGENCY RECORD, AND IT SHOULD CARRY MORE WEIGHT THAN THE WITNESS BESIDE IT. On the evening of 17 November 1986 a Japan Air Lines 747 crossing Alaskan airspace reported an object accompanying it; the FAA investigated, and the paper it generated survives in volume. The Black Vault asked for it in May 2001 and was told in a letter of 27 June 2001 that everything would be destroyed within thirty days; asked again in 2009 and was told it had been destroyed; and then found over 1,500 pages of it at the National Archives in Record Group 237, local identifier 1203, archival identifier 733667. The archive itemises 1,569 pages across thirty-five or more documents: FAA Form 8020-5 Aircraft Incident Record, FAA Form 3112, FAA Form 1600-32-1 interview notes, Captain Terauchi's written statement in Japanese and in English translation, dated transcripts of interviews with all three crew members in January 1987, radar data and computer plots, and a folder of correspondence with Philip Klass and Richard Haines. The agency's conclusion is equally on the record and it is negative: the FAA Alaskan Region's press release of 5 March 1987 states that its experts determined the second radar target was not another aircraft but an uncorrelated primary and beacon return, and that the investigation was complete and would not be pursued further. None of this depends on the Disclosure Project or on any witness, which is exactly why it belongs on this board.

### Why it holds its tier

Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 489 of 1159, score 31). 5 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C0/A0/D2.

### The claims on the record

- **Tier 1 documented.** THE AGENCY'S OWN CONCLUSION. The FAA Alaskan Region press release of 5 March 1987, quoted at length by Klass: FAA experts at the agency's Technical Center in Atlantic City 'determined that a second radar target near the JAL flight... was not another aircraft but was... an uncorrelated primary and beacon [radar transponder] target return. This means that the primary radar signal reflected off the aircraft's [JAL] surface did not correlate exactly with the pulses emitted by the aircraft's radar transponder. This phenomenon is not unusual...' The release concludes: 'The FAA has completed its investigation of JAL flight 1628, and does not intend to pursue it any further.' Source: Philip J. Klass, Skeptics UFO Newsletter (SUN) #68, Summer 2001, 'Dr. Greer's Disclosure Conference Reveals His New Strategy'; PDF downloaded and converted to text in full this session, https://cdn.centerforinquiry.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/29/2022/09/26195512/SUN-68-Summer-2001.pdf, opened 2026-09-19

## Kirkpatrick, 'Here's What I Learned as the U.S. Government's UFO Hunter' (Scientific American)

Kirkpatrick, 'Here's What I Learned as the U.S. Government's UFO Hunter' (Scientific American) is a document on the board; board tier B, documented channel and capability, programme role indicated but not yet nailed to a primary source; dates 2024; axes C0 A1 D2; 5 connections.

In one line: Op-ed, 19 January 2024, seven weeks after leaving AARO.

### What it is

Published 19 January 2024, seven weeks after Kirkpatrick left AARO and seven weeks before the office published the Historical Record Report Volume I he had authored. It is the clearest single statement of the containment thesis in the former director's own voice. Its arguments: the investigation found no evidence of aliens, only allegations circulated repeatedly by UFO claim advocates; the public whistleblowers never provided evidence to AARO despite invitations and are therefore 'suspect' for preferring to be 'sensationalist in the public eye'; the narrative is 'a textbook example of circular reporting, with each person relaying what they heard, but the information often ultimately being sourced to the same small group of individuals'; the claims derive from 'a small group of interconnected believers' influenced by Robert Bigelow and originating in the defunct AATIP; and belief in a statement is proportional to the volume and repetition of its transmission rather than to the facts. The document matters for three reasons. It is a former officeholder attacking named living witnesses in a scientific journal within weeks of departure. It previews the conclusions of an official report not yet published, which is a rollout technique rather than an analysis. And its central mechanism - circular reporting from a small group - is precisely the mechanism the Department would confirm eighteen months later in the Yankee Blue disclosure, except that the small group seeding the belief was the United States Air Force.

### Why it holds its tier

Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 413 of 1159, score 34). 6 connections, 0 of them custody/funding/programmatic, 3 official denials recorded against it. Axes C0/A1/D2.

- **Tier 2 named person on the record.** Kirkpatrick wrote that the crash-retrieval narrative is 'a textbook example of circular reporting' sourced to the same small group of individuals and traceable to Robert Bigelow and AATIP. Source: Sean Kirkpatrick, Scientific American, 19 January 2024
- **Tier 2 named person on the record.** Kirkpatrick wrote that whistleblowers who prefer to be 'sensationalist in the public eye' rather than bring evidence to AARO are 'suspect'. Source: Sean Kirkpatrick, Scientific American, 19 January 2024
- **Tier 3 stated inference.** The op-ed's publication seven weeks before Volume I, by an author who had already left the office, previews the report's conclusions in a venue with scientific prestige and no right of reply - a rollout technique, not an analysis. ## Kirtland AFB / Manzano Weapons Storage Area incident

Kirtland AFB / Manzano Weapons Storage Area incident is a event on the board; board tier B, documented channel and capability, programme role indicated but not yet nailed to a primary source; dates 1980; axes C2 A2 D1; 5 connections.

In one line: 8-9 August 1980, Coyote Canyon and Manzano, Kirtland AFB, New Mexico.

### What it is

On the night of 8 August 1980 three members of the 1608th Security Police Squadron at Kirtland Air Force Base - SSgt Stephen Ferenz, ATC Martin W. Rist and AMN Anthony D. Frazier - watched a very bright light approximately three miles north-north-east of their position perform stop-and-go manoeuvres inconsistent with a helicopter, descend into Coyote Canyon, and later depart straight up at high speed. Shortly after midnight a Sandia Laboratories security guard reported a round disc-shaped object near an alarmed structure, with his radio failing during the encounter. A further incident was recorded on 13 August. AFOSI Special Agent Richard C. Doty documented the reports on a complaint form dated 9 September 1980 under District File No. 8017D93-0/29, describing the 'alleged sighting of unidentified aerial lights in restricted test range'. Manzano is a nuclear weapons storage area. The case matters here because of who is in the file: an Air Force counterintelligence agent, a nuclear storage site security detachment, and a Department of Energy contractor laboratory's own guard force. Within a year the same AFOSI office was running material at Paul Bennewitz. The Kirtland file is where the anomalous-object record, the nuclear weapons complex and the disinformation apparatus visibly overlap.

### Why it holds its tier

Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 357 of 1159, score 36). 5 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C2/A2/D1.

### The claims on the record

- **Tier 1 documented.** A Sandia security guard reported a round disc-shaped object near an alarmed structure at approximately 00:20 on 9 August 1980; his radio malfunctioned during the encounter. Source: AFOSI FOIA release archived by NICAP
- **Tier 1 documented.** AFOSI documented sightings at Kirtland AFB between 8 August and 3 September 1980 on a complaint form dated 9 September 1980 filed by Special Agent Richard C. Doty, District File No. 8017D93-0/29. Source: AFOSI FOIA release archived by NICAP
- **Tier 1 documented.** Independently confirmed this session from the NICAP reproduction of the AFOSI complaint form: the named 1608 Security Police Squadron observers, the Sandia security guard who requested anonymity, and the clock times of 8 to 9 August 1980, together with further observations on 22 August 1980 and a New Mexico State Patrolman on 10 August 1980. The form establishes that uniformed personnel guarding a nuclear weapons storage area reported objects they could not identify and that AFOSI opened a file. IT ESTABLISHES NOTHING ABOUT WHAT THE OBJECTS WERE. Source: AFOSI complaint form, District File No. 8017D93-0/29, reproduced by NICAP from the CUFON archive, https://www.nicap.org/foia_003.htm, opened 2026-09-19
- **Tier 1 documented.** Named observers were SSgt Stephen Ferenz (area supervisor), ATC Martin W. Rist and AMN Anthony D. Frazier of the 1608 Security Police Squadron, reporting at approximately 23:50 on 8 August 1980. Source: AFOSI FOIA release archived by NICAP

## Brasilia, Federal District, Brazil

Brasilia, Federal District, Brazil is a location on the board; board tier C, contextual, real and relevant, no direct programme linkage on the record yet; dates no dates recorded; axes C1 A1 D2; 5 connections.

In one line: Federal capital of Brazil; seat of the Ministry of Defence and the Arquivo Nacional holdings.

### What it is

Brasilia is the seat of the Brazilian federal government and the administrative centre from which the Brazilian Air Force's unidentified aerial phenomena files were released into the Arquivo Nacional, making Brazil one of the few states to have placed military UFO records in a citizen-accessible public archive. The 1986 incident of 19 May, in which Brazilian Air Force fighters were scrambled against multiple radar-tracked objects and the Air Minister subsequently briefed the press, is the country's principal documented case and its records trace back through this capital. Brasilia functions on this board as the control case for what state transparency on this subject actually looks like when it is attempted.

Re-graded C on a global pass (rank 757 of 1159, score 23). 5 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C1/A1/D2.

The Air Force installation in Florida's first congressional district that produced the only UAP incident a member of Congress has personally investigated on site. ## Los Alamos, New Mexico

Los Alamos, New Mexico is a location on the board; board tier B, documented channel and capability, programme role indicated but not yet nailed to a primary source; dates 1943; axes C2 A3 D1; 5 connections.

In one line: Los Alamos National Laboratory; site of the 16 February 1949 green fireballs conference.

### What it is

Los Alamos sits on the Pajarito Plateau in Los Alamos County, New Mexico, and is the site of the laboratory established in 1943 as Project Y of the Manhattan Project, now Los Alamos National Laboratory. Its place on this board rests on two things. First, it is one of the two nuclear design laboratories and therefore one of the small number of American institutions with both the compartmentation architecture and the materials-science capability that a concealed exploitation programme would require; whistleblower accounts collected by AAWSAP and by David Grusch describe materials work distributed across the Department of Energy laboratory complex and its industrial partners, and no document has been produced placing any specific laboratory inside such a programme. Second, and documented, Los Alamos hosted the conference of 16 February 1949 on the green fireballs - the anomalous luminous objects observed repeatedly over northern New Mexico's nuclear installations from December 1948 - attended by Edward Teller and by the University of New Mexico meteoriticist Lincoln LaPaz, whom the Air Force had retained to investigate. LANL's own published account records that the phenomenon was ultimately dismissed as a national security threat, a conclusion that did not prevent the Air Force from standing up Project Twinkle ten months later to instrument it. Los Alamos is thus the first place where American nuclear scientists formally met to discuss unexplained objects over their own facilities, and the meeting is on the laboratory's own record.

### Why it holds its tier

Re-graded B on a global pass (rank 335 of 1159, score 37). 5 connections, 1 of them custody/funding/programmatic. Axes C2/A3/D1.

- **Tier 1 documented.** The 16 February 1949 green fireballs conference was held at Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory and its minutes are held by the National Security Research Center. Source: Los Alamos National Laboratory, 18 November 2024
- **Tier 1 documented.** The Los Alamos Monitor of Sunday 27 June 1982 carried a front-page story by staff writer Terry England, 'LA Man Joins The Jet Set - At 200 Miles An Hour', pages A1 and A8, about a jet-powered Honda built by Bob Lazar, describing him in the paper's own voice as 'a physicist at the Los Alamos Meson Physics Facility'. This is the earliest dated artefact in the Lazar cluster and it predates the UFO claim by seven years. ## Vandenberg Space Force Base, California

Vandenberg Space Force Base, California is a location on the board; board tier B, documented channel and capability, programme role indicated but not yet nailed to a primary source; dates 1941; axes C1 A2 D2; 5 connections.

In one line: Space Force installation near Lompoc, Santa Barbara County; polar-orbit launch, NRO missions, missile defence sites.

### What it is

Vandenberg, on the Santa Barbara County coast near Lompoc, is the United States' west coast space launch installation: it is where polar and sun-synchronous orbits are reached, where National Reconnaissance Office payloads have long gone up, where ICBM test launches down the Western Range originate, and where ground-based missile defence infrastructure sits. It was an Air Force base until it was redesignated a Space Force base in May 2021. Its place on this board comes from sworn congressional testimony rather than from folklore. Jeffrey Nuccetelli, a sixteen-year Air Force veteran who served in security forces at Vandenberg between roughly 2003 and 2005, testified in writing to the House Oversight Task Force on 9 September 2025 that on 14 October 2003 Boeing contractors reported 'a massive, glowing red square silently hovering over two missile defense sites'; that the same night security personnel described 'a massive rectangular craft, larger than a football field' that hovered silently for about 45 seconds before departing at high speed; that a week later a patrol tracked an object inbound from the ocean that descended and vanished, after which the witness 'was threatened and told to kept quiet about the incident'; and that in 2005 a patrol reported a massive triangular craft hovering low over the main base. Two elements make this the most FOIA-actionable location claim in the modern record: Nuccetelli states that 'Official Air Force records documenting it are now held by AARO and the FBI', naming custodians for specific dated incidents at a named installation, and he states that each incident was 'witnessed by multiple personnel, documented, investigated and reported up the chain of command.' Those records have not been produced.

## F. E. Warren AFB, Wyoming
